item.title: John Martyn - Grace and Danger
item.description: The European summer has been exceptionally sunny - so much so that large swaths of forested land have been devoured by hungry fires. While I usually opt for more cheerful and careless music when the sun is out, the current state of affairs leaves room for a more introspective record. Today, I’m bringing you John Martyn’s 1980 Grace & Danger, an album with a sound that fares well in barely lit rooms with a glass of whisky nearby.

item.title: Tatsuro Yamashita - Artisan
item.description:
This summer was a little (too?) ambitious with long distance driving.
Stockholm —> Amsterdam —> Cologne —> Italy —> Cologne —> Dresden —> Stockholm.

Playing CDs in the car was a real highlight.
In our storage container in Amsterdam we stumbled upon old CDs to bring along. Most were 90’s CD’s that I once found on a trash pile in the street some morning (Destiny’s child, Linking Park, Best of Bryan Ferry, etc.), but my collection also contained a souvenir from Japan’s Tower Records store that I never listened to: Tatsuro Yamashita’s 1991 Artisan.

item.title: Opal Sunn - Elastic
item.description: Opal is a gem stone consisting of tiny spheres of the mineral silica that bend light, showing beautiful bright colors when you look at it from different angles. I like to think of this image when listening to the three perspectives of the same song that are on the Elastic EP by Opal Sunn. The same chords and melodies are translated to successively a deep and energetic dancefloor track (Phase 1), a spaced-out dub track (Phase 2), and a meditative piano version (Phase 3). Being into dub music lately, Phase 2 has been on high rotation for me the past weeks.

item.title: Ali Farka Touré With Ry Cooder – Talking Timbuktu
item.description:
I think it must be the heat that’s making me reach for this record again and again recently. Listen to ‘Amandrai’, the sluggish, stubbornly-chugging-along track at the album’s midpoint and tell me it doesn’t sound like it was made to be played strictly at temperatures of 35°C and up.

The album is the result of a collaboration between Malian superstar Ali Farka Touré and the American guitar-chameleon Ry Cooder - recorded at the latter’s studio when the former had traveled from his home in Timbuktu to the US for a tour.

item.title: Widowspeak - Roses
item.description: If you are looking for the soundtrack to your Sunday morning, look no further: I’ve got you. The Brooklyn duo Widowspeak has been making music for over a decade, carving out their own cosy little nook in the heavily occupied dreamy indie space. Although their music is always warm and homey, new album Roses sounds like it’s made from a mental space that is both confident and comfortable. Very impressive, considering that the duo - who also happen to be a couple - welcomed a baby daughter last year. Catch them on tour this autumn - I’ve seen them multiple times now and I’ve never been disappointed.

item.title: Tensen Park - MythStream
item.description:
Vanity press alert!!!

This week’s listening is about my own album, MythStream which got released yesterday.
I told myself it’s okay to write about it, if we can treat this as a retrospective of everything I’ve recommended before. Maybe it makes sense to describe music with music for once. Having this as a medium now, all the words I’ve written can feel a bit like using dance to describe architecture.

item.title: Mytron - Propellor
item.description:
“I got sugar for your monkeeheeheehee”

That line is stuck in my head since a dear friend send me the track Sugar by Mytron some weeks ago. Not knowing the artist, I played the entire album and been revisiting it regularly. Both the lyrics and the music sound like someone having a lot of fun making music, not taking life too seriously while still delivering great dance music in a dark space disco style that reminds me of Axel Boman. Another seemingly random but convincing tune is the title track Propeller that includes the German lyrics: “ Wollen sie ein Flugzeug sein, geben Sie Propeller ein.”

item.title: Way Dynamic - Massive Shoe
item.description:
With my summer plans taking shape, I’m looking forward particularly to being on the road (again) - music always plays a central role in these in-between moments for me, driving in a car or sitting on the train. My go-to albums of the summer have much better odds of sticking around and becoming long-term go-to’s than those I discover in spring, fall or winter.

A real big favorite from last year’s summer trips has recently found its way back to my (almost) daily rotation: Massive Shoe by Way Dynamic. This one charmed me on the first listen, immediately comfortably familiar-sounding, but drawing from enough different inspirations that it’s fresh too (I’ll let you play the “oh hey that sounds like [X]" -game yourself, instead of saying what it reminds me of).

item.title: Judee Sill - Judee Sill
item.description: Judee Sill grew up in LA’s Studio City as the daughter of a man who imports exotic animals for the neighbouring studios. Truly an environment with many imaginative stories around - some of which may have inspired her to take up a ‘career’ of armed robberies targeting gas stations and liquor stores as a late teenager. Thanks to the reform school she was sent to after, she learned to play the church organ well and decided to try her luck in the music industry. David Geffen - no stranger to the movie business as he founded DreamWorks later in life - recognised her talent and signed her into his newly founded Asylum label, which went on to release music by Joni Mitchell, The Eagles, Jackson Browne, Bon Dylan and Warren Zevon.

item.title: Gregory Uhlmann, Josh Johnson, Sam Wilkes - Uhlmann Johnson Wilkes
item.description:
Happy Easter folks! I’m happy to share that today’s Listening fits the Easter holiday theme quite well. It’s described as ‘a jazz-informed take on progressive electro-acoustic chamber music’ and could be something that you might play on the couch with the family these days. For me it’s surely been the winding-down music for the weekend afternoons the last few months.

While the soundscapes could take some space sometimes, (many parts are live-improvisations), the warmth and beauty you get from some sections is unparalleled. They land on these very pretty, intimate sections of warm melodies, played so softly.

item.title: Hannes - God Bless Sweden
item.description:
I found out about Hannes because Benny Sings once said in an interview he’s a big admirer. I think the artists show a lot of resemblance, they’re both great at writing little pop songs.

God Bless Sweden came out last month, but contains some of Hannes’ earlier work — the popular song Stockholmsvy was released in 2022. Please don’t be misled by the intense intro tune, and be sure to play the second half of the album where hits are.

item.title: Otto Benson - Peanut
item.description:
I’m not entirely sure anymore, but I think I picked this one up from the NTS Breakfast Show with Flo. In any case, that was five or six weeks ago and I’m still finding myself clicking play every couple of days - I love it when that happens! Somehow this record scratches a certain itch for me, satisfies a particular type of musical craving that keeps me coming back.

The opening track Mr. Peanut stands apart from the rest of the album and functions a little bit like an ouverture, announcing the moody-but-playful vibe of these 10 tracks and inviting you to specifically pay attention to the carefully crafted textures on display. What I mean is: the melodies are pretty simple, but each instrument has a very specific sound quality that excites me. Starting with the wonky guitar and bloopy bass, then introducing a super reverb-y marimba which turns into an ethereal-sounding synth and finally just one high-pitched bell sound - it’s the layering of these textures that makes the album for me.

item.title: Neil Young - Tonight's the Night
item.description:
The other day, I stumbled upon an interview where Gillian Welch & Dave Rawlings – a duo I hold in very high esteem - were both asked to name their top 5 albums ever. It struck me that they both included Neil Young’s Tonight’s the Night on their list. Even though I consider myself a Young enthusiast, this album had somehow always escaped my attention.

I’m grateful to Welch and Rawlings for directing my attention to this record, because it’s been on high rotation ever since. The album was written and recorded in the aftermath of two people close to Young passing away from heroin overdoses. The grief is almost tangible, as is the consolation that can be found when grieving together. As mentioned by the band in interviews afterwards, the recording of these songs was accompanied by the intake of substantial amounts of booze. This is reflected in the loose, live feel of the record and in the lyrics to Borrowed Tune, where Young mentions stealing a melody from a Rolling Stones song because he’s too wasted to write his own.

item.title: Jeremiah Chiu & Sofia Honer - Different Rooms
item.description:
Music-wise, this time of the year is my favorite time.
It’s all thanks to the end of the year lists that give me a proper tailwind.
One of these lists, brought my attention to Jeremiah Chiu & Sofia Honer’s Different Rooms.

For some reason, I completely missed this release, even though I absolutely loved their previous work, Recordings from the Åland Islands.

Different Rooms goes deep. It doesn’t force a specific mood too much, but if it does it’s kind of nostalgic, and psychedelic. The songs are like an ocean of synthesizer and acoustic instruments (often violin (a little subdued, not the annoying kind)), and the vibe is sort of implicitly rhythmic, almost hypnotic, through repeating motifs, not percussion per se.

item.title: Chaos in the CBD - Midnight in Peckham
item.description:
No, CBD does not refer to the stuff you get at the smart shop. It means Central Business District, a term commonly used in New Zeeland (and Australia) when talking about a city center. The two brothers in Chaos in the CBD hail from Auckland, and moved to London shortly after the duo was formed. As for the title, Peckham is a neighbourhood in London.

Having that out of the way, let’s talk music. I bought this record for a good friend in Scotland, at a lovely dance music store in Glasgow called Rub-A-Dub. I picked it because it’s dance music that is great for listening at home. It’s easy on the ear, but never boring. The chords and melodies are jazzy and soothing, but combined with off beat rhythms they become hypnotising. It uses cliché in a way that turns out interesting — the title song could have been a corny brass house tune, but accompanied with lo-fi drums it sounds convincingly different. Ten years after its release, Midnight in Peckham still hits the spot for me.

item.title: James Krivchenia - Performing Belief
item.description: When the winter is wintering , I find my listening habits going two ways. On some days I lean into the wintery-ness, listening to moody, atmospheric, sparse sounds - appreciating the slowing down that comes with the frosty season. But when the (pleasant) slowing down turns into (dreadful) fatigue and lethargy, that’s when I need a record that goes in the exact opposite direction, a record that’s energetic and upbeat and that makes me want to get up and move around and get things done.

item.title: Billie Marten - Dog Eared
item.description: First of all, happy New Year from us at Listenings! We have been all over the place over the past year - chronologically, that is. We have recommended some of our favourite 2025 releases and dug up some earlier pearls, ranging from 1969 up to 2023. Thanks for sticking with us, we hope you enjoy listening to these albums as much as we enjoy recommending them.

item.title: Gábor Szabó – 1969
item.description:
Last week, Spotify bought WhoSampled. For those who do not know, it’s a massive community-driven database of information on reused music. Spotify says it will add WhoSampled’s data to the platform through a forthcoming “SongDNA” feature. The internet’s busiest music nerd, Anthony Fantano, is concerned about the purchase, most importantly because it might give major labels more power to earn money through credits.

The moments I enjoy samples the most are when I stumble upon the original and it turns out to be better— especially when the original is on an album full of beautiful songs. This happened when I heard Gábor Szabó’s “Stormy”, which you’ll instantly recognise from John Legend’s “Save Room”. Gábor himself is not afraid of reusing music either, as most of the songs on “1969” are covers. As can be read on WhoSampled.

item.title: Headache - Thank You For Almost Everything
item.description:
Headache is a project by Vegyn, the elusive producer who became friends with James Blake in a nightclub and ended up working with Frank Ocean on Blonde and Endless. Ever since, he has been releasing some great albums, but this second album under his Headache moniker really is something else. The warm-blooded productions are vintage Vegyn, but what’s new is the spoken word poetry lyrics over it all.

Despite the fact that Headache’s voice is obviously AI-generated, the lyrics are so human and real that this album can really hit the spot. Perfect for listening on headphones in a train while watching the world go by.

item.title: YS - Burn
item.description:
It’s super cool how this album just came out, but what a time-machine it really is. On the first listen I got transported into my favorite trip-hop-soundtracked 90’s high octane movies.
The sound is reminiscent of Massive Attack, Board of Canada, Portishead, and some Moby in the mix. Still it’s doing its own authentic thing with it. Hope it’s a sign that trip-hop is making a comeback!

~ Mark

item.title: Single Gun Theory - Millions, Like Stars in My Hands
item.description: When thinking about the plethora of new music releases that flood us on a daily basis, I sometimes find myself nostalgically wondering what it would have been like to live on the other side of the world in the pre-internet age, waiting for a weekly shipment of new albums considered good enough to take up precious space. I would have suspected that records and trends would take longer to reach the land down under, but the album I am recommending this Monday morning proves that the Aussies were really on trend, despite the physical distance.

item.title: Huerco S. - For Those Of You Who Have Never (And Also Those Who Have)
item.description:
For almost a month I’ve mainly been listening to dub-techno mixes. They’re great, but also symptomatic of spending too little time to discover new stuff.

For the past week though, I’ve been playing this really interesting album “For Those Of You Who Have Never (And Also Those Who Have)” on repeat.
This album was always half skipped-over when I just discovered the musical corner where ambient / experimental intersects with club music from labels like Peak Oil, West Mineral ltd, 3XL.

item.title: Caribou – Honey
item.description:
I don’t think this is Caribou’s best album, and I didn’t listen to it for a while after hearing the first time. However, after seeing the man on Best Kept Secret this year, I was impressed how well the music works live. Last weekend, a friend gave me the record as a birthday present and I got to revisit it.

Something special happened when I reached the third track ‘Volume’. I got a beautiful flash back to Rainbow Disco Club festival in Japan last year, when Four Tet played it in the beginning of his set. This tune was a great start of a long night full of energy on the dance floor. The recording of Four Tet is on SoundCloud, check it out.

item.title: Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band - New Threats From The Soul
item.description:
Last Wednesday, MJ Lenderman & The Wind played a stellar show in Amsterdam. As I suspect many of you are already familiar with his tiptop record Manning Fireworks (if not, go check it out), today’s newsletter is about the equally impressive support act, Ryan Davis & The Roadhouse Band.

As touring becomes more expansive and more of a hassle, it is a great privilege to see a support act bring a six-piece band to the stage, and an excellent one at that. Ryan Davis’ vocals are reminiscent of a less angry Matt Berninger while the band’s sound could be described as Songs: Ohia-inspired with the rhythm section of The War on Drugs. It is a pleasure to hear a band that sounds so comfortable on stage, a vibe they managed to hold on their latest album, recommended here today.

item.title: N Kramer & Magnus Bang Olsen - Pastoral Blend
item.description:
This album was sent by a friend for its beautiful album cover.
I agreed; an album cover at its finest.

As for the sound: It is warm and organic. The disassembled and smooth slide guitar together with the synths is overwhelmingly peaceful. It sort of meanders. Not in a blissed-out kind of way, but complex, organic, and interesting improvisations.

The first time it clicked for me was when reading the most wholesome article (written in 1910) about the magic of having a dog as companion. This feeling of love in the article showed me it was this same feeling present in the music that made me enjoy it so much. The favorite line was:

item.title: Todd Terje - It's Album Time
item.description: This album recommendation might be old for some. Others might only know the hit song ‘Inspector Norse’, which was very popular at parties over ten years ago. ‘It’s Album Time’ (2014) is one of those dance LP’s I often play entirely, as the songs smoothly transition into the next, and have a coherent Space Disco sound. Also, I get reminded of this album a lot when I hear similarities in other music. Like last weekend, at Parallel festival near Barcelona. Denato Dozzy played ‘Apex Break’ by Torn Hawk and Black Deer (2025), and the crazy arps immediately made me think of Terje’s ‘Preben Goes to Acapulco’. When I shared this reference with a friend, he agreed and showed me that in turn Terje’s track was based on ‘Solstice’ by Brian Bennet (1978). I guess we live in a postmodern remake culture, that just keeps on giving. Speaking of remakes, be sure to check out the original version of ‘Johnny and Mary’ by Robert Palmer, which is nicely covered by Bryan Ferry of Roxy Music on ‘It’s Album Time’.

item.title: Foxwarren - 2
item.description:
“Foxwarren” is a small town in western Manitoba, Canada and although I would have loved to tell you all about the interesting stuff I’ve encountered on my recent Streetview exploration, this is a music newsletter and Foxwarren is also a band.

It’s the band that was already fronted by singer Andy Shauf before his excellent 2016 breakthrough solo album “The Party”, and I’m glad that despite Shauf his solo success, the band still put out their debut album in 2018. I am even more delighted that this album has received a successor this year.

item.title: Skee Mask - Compro
item.description:
Skee Mask is known for a bunch of amazing releases on Ilian Tape. This is his second album, and it’s incredible.

The cover says a lot; Misty, obscured, and deep. It’s easy to get lost in the sauce with the lush atmospheric sounds. The beats keep things tightly together though. It has a sort of dub-techno, ambient techno feel, but at the same time this meticulous hip-hop style chopped-up beats give it some real magic.

item.title: Wilson Tanner - Legends
item.description: While writing this, I’m in that hazy state of happiness and tiredness, as it’s the Monday after three days of Best Kept Secret festival. I’m re-watching the concert registrations on my phone, while lying in sun. Little kids are jumping in the water next to my house, and I’m about to follow. The soundtrack that fits my mood is the latest album of Wilson Tanner. You might know one of the duo, under the name of Andras. Together the two Aussies create peaceful ambient, that makes you feel like being on a vineyard in rural Perth.

item.title: Andrea - Due In Color
item.description:
When I first saw the album cover, I remembered taking a similar photo at the exact same place: Joshua Tree Park, Cholla cactus garden. More relevant: I remember driving the long desert road with the car speakers blasting Four Tet’s New Energy.

Maybe my mind played tricks on me by associating the images, but I really think the that Due in Color hits that exact same note for me.

item.title: Amen Dunes - Freedom
item.description:
Today, on May 5th, we celebrate freedom in The Netherlands. Exactly 80 years ago the German occupation ended.

Last week in Scotland I was reminded of the country’s long fight for independence, when I learned about a statue of William Wallace from the movie Braveheart, as played by Mel Gibson, in the city of Stirling. The word ‘Freedom’ is written on the base of the statue, referring to the famous quote “they may take our lives, but they’ll never take our freedom”. Because the thing is pretty ugly, and has the face of Mel Gibson, the Scots ridiculed and vandalised it. To protect it, a fence was placed around it. The result: an encased Braveheart figure standing for freedom. Oh, the irony.

item.title: Saya Gray - SAYA
item.description:
Now that the sunny weather seems to have left us, it is time to bring back those vibes with Saya Gray’s deliciously breezy, yet intricately layered latest album, released last February. The melodies are both meticulous and meandering and fit in perfectly with the crisp and layered production. It’s poppy, organic, clever and effortless at the same time.

I may seem a bit over-generous with the adjectives, but I believe they are justified. In the first track, Saya tells us she doesn’t fall in love in the spring time - easier said than done when, on this album, there’s so much to fall for.

item.title: Florian T M Zeisig - Planet Inc
item.description: For some reason, a couple of mornings ago, I had Planet Inc playing on my iPhone speaker, and forgot all about it while continuing tinkering on a side-project. It was magical. Only when the album finished I realized what a deep trip I was in. Listening to music without knowing that I was, was like my head-space made it by itself. It made me think of the movie Inception; conveying an idea while ‘unconscious’ can convey the strongest message.

item.title: Letta Mbulu - In The Music The Village Never Ends
item.description: About ten years ago during Afro heyday, virtually every DJ in Amsterdam carried the down-tempo ‘Normalizo’ of this album. I heard it so often, I couldn’t listen to the South African Letta Mbulu for a long while. However, recently I started playing the album again because of the last track, ‘The Village’. It takes me back to a memorable moment at the end of a beautiful night in the basement of De School. At around 6 in the morning, after an hour of spacey twisted techno, this uplifting call-and-response tune woke me up and let me leave the club with a big smiling face.

item.title: man oh man! - Martin Luke Brown
item.description: For today’s recommendation, we go back in time sonically to the early 2010s, when the indie scene was dominated by the subdued, lo-fi sounds of Youth Lagoon, Unknown Mortal Orchestra and Mac DeMarco. Nowadays, such sounds are hard to come by. For those of you with some nostalgia towards this era I, I found an English Gen Z’er who completely embraced this vibe and wrote some stellar songs basking in 2010s glory. Unoriginal? Maybe. But there definitely is enough freshness in these songs, and yesterday I found out they work extremely well when listening when spring is in the air.

item.title: Il Quadro di Troisi - Il Quadro di Troisi
item.description: Il Quadro di Troisi is Eva Geist and Denato Dozzy. Two Italian producers with a fine taste; just look at them lounging in the curved couch on the cover of their self-titled debut album (2020). A combination that results in dreamy vocals and trippy arpeggiators. The tracks are very much loop based, just like Dozzy’s solo techno productions. But slower, and structured like pop songs. At times, the album even includes classic Italo Disco elements. For instance the bass of ‘Raggio Verde’.

item.title: Downstairs People - DSP
item.description:
Last few days I’ve been compiling a mix-tape for Amsterdam based music platform ‘Far Blue’.
They operate under this quote and I’m gonna shamelessly CTRL-C+CTRL-V the thing in, because it’s beautiful:

“The world is blue at its edges and in its depths… For many years I have been moved by the blue at the far edge of what can be seen, that color of horizons, of remote mountain ranges, of anything far away. The color of that distance is the color of an emotion, the color of solitude and of desire, the color of there seen from here, the color of where you are not. And the color of where you can never go. For the blue is not in the place those miles away at the horizon… Blue is the color of longing for the distances you never arrive in, for the blue world.”
- Rebecca Solnit from ‘A Field Guide to Getting Lost’

item.title: Sylvie - Sylvie
item.description:
Sometimes, I just want music to be soothing—no weird noises, no dissonance, just beautiful sounds to ease me through. At the same time, I can be quite critical of soothing music: it should not be too cheesy, too easy, or too sterile. Records that strike that perfect balance are rare. However, for today’s recommendation, Sylvie’s self-titled album, I found one.____

The album was created when Ben Schwab (who also plays in Drugdealer) found some old cassettes in the attic of his parents’ house, containing recordings from his dad’s band in the ’70s. Loving the vibe, he gathered some friends to record an album in the same spirit. Though multiple vocalists appear (Sam Burton, Marina Allen, and Ben’s dad), the album feels like a unified whole, radiating warmth. Soothing in just the right way. Enjoy.

item.title: Ike Zwanikken - Greed Gave Me A Lily
item.description:
Now why I love this album so much might be the same reason as why I’m blown away by David Lynch movies; They never fully disclose the situation. There’s just a deep unknown with different forces at play, which I’ll never understand. I’m just somewhere on the surface of it, blissfully being pulled along, meandering between scary / loving / funny.

Not that it’s the same vibe, but this album does the same thing to me. It’s warm, nostalgic, weirdly alien, and then loving. Just new worlds to explore. There’s nothing really like it.

item.title: Black Devil Disco Club - Black Devil Disco Club
item.description:
During Christmas, a dinner at a friend’s place ended in dancing in the kitchen and eventually moving to the club for a long night out. One thing that got us going was the record player in that kitchen and the extensive vinyl collection of the owner.

The record that did it for me, and which I played again during the hangover, was Black Devil Disco Club’s first release from 1978. This six-track EP is a contiguous trip down the depths of disco hell. You get taken along on a kick-snare ride with both refreshing and disturbing synthesizer noises and echoing sing-alongs. I was surprised to find out this record is from the 70’s, as many of the sounds can be still be heard in modern dance music today.

item.title: Gena Rose Bruce - Deep Is The Way
item.description:
For this weekend’s pick, we venture all the way out to the land down under. Although Gena Rose Bruce is technically a singer-songwriter, this album has too much grit and schwung to be classified as another “girl-with-guitar”-record.

Hailing from Melbourne, she made the excellent “Can’t Make You Love Me” in 2019, an album that somehow managed to grab the attention of Bill Callahan, resulting in a gorgeous duet on this week’s recommendation, “Deep Is The Way”. Perfect for Sundays.

item.title: Mr YT - Brand New Day
item.description:
Today’s listening is Mr YT (Yuji Takenouchi)’s Brand New Day.

The first song, ‘Morning’, is just unbelievable. Such a journey. ’Nite’ is a close second. For both it’s quite hard to put a finger on which time they really belongs in. Could be because Takenouchi scored some iconic and futuristic video games for Sony, which must’ve conjured up otherwordly scenes in his mind on a daily basis.

The other songs are cool housey danceable tunes, which hint at the album’s creation time (1997) way better. Also very cool.

item.title: Discovery Zone - Remote Control
item.description: Do you remember the early days of the internet, when surfing the web sounded like visiting a parallel universe and AI was seen as something with supernatural powers? That’s the vibe I get from listening to JJ Weihl (New York) aka Discovery Zone. Last week I went to her concert in Cinetol, together with fellow Listenings writer Mark, and dear Listenings listener Isa. The setup was amazing, with Discovery Zone standing behind a see-through screen on which nostalgic cyberspace animations were beamed throughout the show. Imagine flying dolphins, geometrical pulsating patterns and lively color streams. A well designed mix between irony and beauty. The whole experience left me feeling excited for a time to come yet already passed.

item.title: Songs: Ohia - Magnolia Electric Co.
item.description:
Early this summer, I found myself driving along the endless but gorgeous roads of the Scottish coast, exploring the country’s outer isles. Thanks to its fickle weather, Scotland is no destination for the average sun-and-beach vacation—it actually felt like fall had already arrived.

One day, when the sun was shining but rain clouds were starting to roll in, our road trip soundtrack needed an adjustment. We chose Magnolia Electric Co. (2003) by the late Jason Molina, released under his Songs: Ohia moniker. This dark, compelling album has a rare clarity and beauty, recorded live in the studio so it almost feels like you’re in the audience at an intense show. It’s perfect for a rainy day—just like the ones we are about to see plenty of.

item.title: M. Sage - The Wind of Things
item.description:
M. Sage’s The Wind Of Things is an album dear to my heart.

I once used it as a soundtrack when reading John Steinbeck’s Travels With Charley , which is a heartwarming story of John and his dog Charley road-tripping the US in the 60’s. It pairs so well because The Wind of Things is heartwarming as well.

The music is a series of ambient soundscapes. And when you think of ambient you can imagine lushy synthesizers and over-exaggerated reverb exploring the ether. That’s not the case here though.

item.title: John Maus - We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves
item.description:
Last week I went to Paradiso in Amsterdam to see John Maus for the first time. I had not listened to his music since the release of his album ‘We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves’ in 2011, and I had no idea what to expect from the show.

When support act Pol finished and took their guitars, drums and synthesisers, all that was left was a laptop in the middle of the stage. Soon John walked up and kneeled in front of the computer, turning his back to the audience, and hit the play button. He then jumped up and went raving and running like a maniac across the stage, shouting into the microphone over the prerecorded music, inviting the audience to shout along. The scene reminded me of a pumped up priest spreading God’s energy in a church. This thing repeated every time he put on the next song, until he was soaking wet from sweat.

item.title: Cleo Sol - Lost Angel
item.description:
I was planning on recommending some serious, lightly sad autumn album to usher in the new season, but this September weekend is giving off very summery vibes here in Amsterdam. That’s why I’ve decided to go with that flow and share this perfect late-summer album with you.

Some of you might recognise Cleo Sol’s voice because she is the most prominent vocalist of the elusive SAULT, a somewhat mysterious collective of musicians helmed by producer Inflo. If you haven’t yet had the pleasure of exploring their work, check out their irresistible track ‘Wildfires’ for a taste.

item.title: Loidis - One Day
item.description:
One Day was released in August, and has succeeded in soundtracking my late-summer.
It’s been hard to miss in the circles where I browse the web. Likely because I’ve been a fan of the artist’s other alias Huerco S, which created this introspective depth-plunging ambient album, For Those Of You Who Have Never (And Also Those Who Have).

On One Day , the ambient makes place for house-y grooves, but the ambient remains in its undercurrents. It has this four-to-the-floor beat, and characteristic house sounds, but those are the only genre-conform aspects of it. Ive read it being called Outsider House.

item.title: Don Ray - The Garden of Love
item.description: This is my go-to record pick when I’m home alone cooking, cleaning or dancing. It’s just sitting there with its bright coloured square letters, shouting to be pulled out of the cabinet. You might know the opening track Got to Have Loving, if not the original then maybe the highly sought-after edit by Oceanic, for which he took a sample from the amazing 2-minute break halfway the track. However, often I prefer to put the record on my turntable B-side up, starting with the the dripping arpeggio’s of Standing in the Rain, followed by the instant happiness of Garden of Love, ending with the slow but powerful My Desire.

item.title: Noami Sharon - Obsidian
item.description: Last weekend on Down The Rabbit Hole, I was eating very tasty fish and chips from Zijpe Stijl in between the performances from RAYE and Eefje de Visser. Once home, I realised that on that very moment, Naomi Sharon was playing on the other end of the festival. In the weeks before I had played her album Obsidian repeatedly, wanting to check her out. Oh well, that’s how it goes. I now like to assure myself that she probably didn’t match up to the shows of RAYE and Eefje anyway, which were amazing.

item.title: Françoise Hardy - La Question
item.description:
When Françoise Hardy passed away last month, I must admit my knowledge of her work was limited to her canonical “Tous les garçons et les filles”, first heard in French class when I was 13 years old, and “Comment te dire adieu”.

As much as I appreciated these two airy songs evoking sepia images of a pre-tourism-boom Paris, I had no idea about the cultural context that gave rise to these songs and their counterparts like France Gall’s “Poupee de cire poupee de son”.

item.title: Shabason, Krgovich, Sage
item.description:
I haven’t just streamed, but always felt a deep urge to buy almost every release with Joseph Shabason on it. He makes this instrumental, organic, murky, emotionally complex, psychedelic music.
Not so easy to describe, but his signature is his saxophone sound that doesn’t really sound like saxophone at all, and combined with these smooth 90’s keyboard sounds.

Then he had this incredible collaboration ~2 years ago with Nicholas Krgovich, which added vocals to the mix. Camiel and I actually listened to the first single of this record (I’m so happy with my little dog) a bunch on our road trip through the US.

item.title: John Talabot - Fin
item.description:
Two weeks ago on Lentekabinet, I was somehow dissapointed to find out John Talabot had jumped on the trance train that has been riding for a bit too long. Along with DJ’s such as Job Jobse and Young Marco, Talabot is speeding way beyond the 130 limit.

I know I sound like a grumpy old man now…

Luckily, at home I can play the low BPMs of 2011’s release ‘Fin’. A true classic in it’s genre, according to many of my dancefloor friends. It takes me back to the days my feet could still meet the beat and makes me hopeful for a downtempo revival after the superfast music hype is over.

item.title: The Kills - Midnight Boom
item.description:
****

Earlier this month I’ve had the pleasure to see The Kills play Paradiso. Even though the album they released this year was quite decent, I will make the sorry judgment that their creative peak lies in the past. No real shame, as this is how things go for most. After this bad news I do have some good news for them too: their 2008 breakthrough record ‘Midnight Boom’ sounds as cool as ever, showing its first signs of timelessness. After their first two albums being firmly rooted in bluesy and grainy guitar sounds, this record embraces the available technology in a way that clearly sparked creativity while even enhancing their already sizeable natural cool. The deliciously sleazy U.R.A Fever, the upbeat Cheap & Cheerful, the positively shrill Tape Song - true delights. Especially recommended during a bike ride in the dark.

item.title: Mixmaster Morris, Jonah Sharp, Haruomi Hosono - Quiet Logic
item.description:
Last 2 weeks I was on a little roadtrip through Japan. Many albums, mixes and songs were played, but the greatest discovery for me during this time was Quiet Logic.

Haruomi Hosono is one of my all time favorite artists, and I’ve been following the WRWTFWW records label for a while. When they announced it I had to get it. Albeit also slightly because of the gorgeous album cover.

item.title: Various Artists – Heisei No Oto (Japanese Left-Field Pop From The CD Age, 1989-1996)
item.description:
In a few days I’ll be in Japan, together with fellow Listenings-writer Mark. I’m very excited to walk through the largest city on Earth, climb the 100,000 years old Mount Fuji and be surprised by a unique culture.

Evidently I’ve been listening to a lot of great Japanese music lately. The Heisei No Noto compilation by Music from Memory hits the spot for me. It contains many well composed dreamy ambient tracks, that take me to far away places yet to discover. There are also two more beat driven, almost Krautrocky, tunes I especially recommend you to listen to. Pi Po Pa by Yosui Inoue will probably unconsciously make you sing along to the three words of the title, leaving you with a feeling that everything will be alright. On Harai, Keisuke Sakurai sounds like the Japanese brother of Shaggy (you’re right Simon). Mr. Bombastic from Tokyo does a great job mumbling over a fine piano house beat.

item.title: Portishead - Roseland NYC live
item.description: Portishead has always been an elusive band. After their ’94 breakthrough with the relatively easygoing, vibey Dummy (featuring bona fide radio hit Glory Box) and the self-titled ’97 follow-up they disappeared from the radar, only to return in 2008 with the relentless, uncompromising album Third. This release was followed by a tour that can be seen as a victory march, leaving audiences in awe and introducing the sheer live force of this group to new, young listeners like myself. Back then, I couldn’t find the magic of what I encountered on stage in their first two studio albums, but I did catch it in their ’98 live recording from New York City’s Roseland Ballroom, where the band was accompanied by a 28-piece orchestra. Last month, a remastered version was released – a perfect opportunity to relive this monument of a live album.

item.title: Shinetiac - Not All Who Wander Are Lost
item.description:
Lately I’ve been listening a lot to releases by the Kansas label West Mineral Ltd.

Initially discovered through Purelink, featured last time by me, who shared some of their inspirations in an interview.

The label’s been releasing some real top-notch psychedelic, experimental, electronic music, ranging from ambient to more beat-driven energy levels. Very interesting, complex, and inspiring to my own music productions as well.

The release I wanted to highlight today by Shinetiac, Not all Who Wander Are Lost, has been quite dear to me in the last 2 months. It’s hard to pinpoint what exact mood it conveys. At some points it’s deeply soothing, but never fully, sometimes feeling lost, while being kind of nostalgic or sad at the same time. It’s really quite complex when you listen deeply, a real treat for the brain, so alienating that I feel human.

item.title: The Boney King of Nowhere – Everybody Knows (2024)
item.description: When I ride my bicycle through the Utrechtsestraat in Amsterdam, I often make two stops. At the thrift shop in Kerkstraat, and at the second-hand house and techno bins of Concerto record store. There are always gems to be found in both places, which I perhaps should have kept to myself. Anyway, earlier this month I walked into Concerto and was greeted by the music the salesperson had put on. Moving on to the second-hand section, I turned around and asked at the counter if this was something by Radiohead that I did not know of. I have a group of friends who are die-hard Radiohead fans, and they will probably judge me for this, but I’m one of those listeners who structurally ignore a few of their albums.

item.title: Linda Perhacs – Parallelograms (1970)
item.description:
Spotify, Bandcamp

At its western edge, Los Angeles borders the rugged hills of Topanga State Park. In the 1920s Hollywood stars found refuge in the quaint canyon. The 60s brought in the creatives of that time - Neil Young wrote most of his After the Goldrush there. Another resident those days was Linda Perhacs, a twenty something Californian working as a dental hygienist in Beverly Hills, writing songs in Topanga in her spare time.

item.title: Purelink - Signs
item.description:
Spotify, Bandcamp

Listenings will kick off with Signs by Purelink.

It’s my favorite/most listened to album of last year and it would feel weird not to choose it.

First time I really listened to it closely was on a flight, having the album on repeat, spacing out, half slumbering, half gazing at the clouds. Not sure how many listening cycles I had but it really stuck with me since then.

item.title: Hello!
item.description:
Hello esteemed friend,

Fear not, for this no random spam - this is an e-mail from Mark and Camiel who subscribed you to this list because we genuinely think you want to receive this mail. For many of us, discovering new music has increasingly been limited to whatever spotify or youtube algorithms come up with, while playing music has often been reduced to a soundtrack for something else you are doing. Through this new mailing we will recommend one album every two weeks. Take some time to immerse yourself in this album and, if you feel like it, share your experiences with us in the Discord-group. Read our full manifesto here and let us know what you think - recommendations, improvements or other comments are always welcome.
